title: Joint SLA Admission and Risk Allocation for Cloud Resource Provisioning
comment: Author accepted manuscript for the AICCC 2026 proceedings. The version of record will be available in the ACM Digital Library. 14 pages, 1 figure. Yihua Xu and Jize Li contributed equally and share first authorship
summary: Cloud controllers must reserve enough CPU and memory to meet demand without leaving too much capacity idle. Under a shared service-level agreement (SLA), a shortage of CPU or memory (considered as resource) counts toward the same limit. Dividing the allowed shortage risk between them changes how much extra capacity each need. We study this choice when forecast-error histories are short or correlated over time. Our controller compares different approaches to split the allowed shortage risk between resources. For each split, the controller uses historical forecast errors to determine how much extra capacity to reserve. It checks whether the history is enough to support that split and its consistency across different parts of the history. Among the splits that pass, it chooses the one with the lowest combined cost of shortages and idle capacity. Otherwise, the controller continues serving the workload with a calibrated fallback. In our simulation, we set a joint SLA target of sufficient CPU and memory in at least 95% of time slots and used 192 hours of historical forecast errors to structure the controller. Compared with always using fallback, the controller reduced the time slots allocation with either of the resource shortage by 1.04 percentage points on average. This reduction came with a 0.0091 increase in normalized cost from shortages and idle capacity. In the Bitbrains trace, five nonoverlapping test windows did not provide clear evidence of whether shortages increased or decreased. We also examine how execution delays and adjustment limits affect this trade off.

title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
summary:
LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates.
  We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.

title: Specification-Grounded Adaptive Triage and Formal Invariant Exclusion Synthesis for Autonomous Silicon Coverage Closure
summary:
Closing the final 5%-15% of code and functional coverage remains a major schedule bottleneck in silicon tapeouts. Existing LLM-based coverage closure loops feed raw uncovered RTL lines or branches directly into iterative prompts, failing on industrial subsystems due to: (1) token and context explosion from querying thousands of correlated holes independently; (2) illegal stimulus that violates cross-signal invariants and yields dirty coverage; and (3) unsafe exclusion hallucination on structurally unreachable dead code.
  We present ARGUS (Autonomous Reachability & Guided Unified Stimulus), a specification-grounded, dual-regime coverage closure and formal exclusion synthesis engine. ARGUS mines microarchitectural specs and SystemVerilog Assertions into a formal Block Contract (C), then runs adaptive Macro-Clustering vs. Micro-Surgery triage gated by a per-module hole-density threshold (tau): dense modules collapse correlated holes into root-cause mode, FSM, and backpressure clusters, while sparse modules use AST and loop-domain reachability to separate reachable corners from provably unreachable invariants. Directed tests pair with bit-exact golden scoreboards, and unreachable invariants emit tool-native .el exclusions with formal proofs.
  Across five core benchmarks -- three open-source LowRISC OpenTitan IPs (uart_core, i2c_core, aes_cipher_core) and two commercial AI accelerator Tensor Layout Converter datapaths (53 SV modules, 376,127 coverage points) -- plus a 2,626-module industrial interconnect subsystem, ARGUS triages 2,626 modules in 0.265 s, cuts token usage by 27.2x to >180x, achieves zero dirty merges via 3-step sanity gating, and reaches 99.32%-100.0% effective coverage with 0 false exclusions across 21,071+ proven exclusions.

title: Improved (Minimum) Spanning Tree Construction in the HYBRID Model
comment: 26 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Full version of a paper to appear at OPODIS 2026
summary: In the HYBRID$_0$ model, vertices exchange $O(\log n)$-bit messages in synchronous rounds, both along input edges (local communication) and directly to vertices whose IDs they know (global communication). The local capacity is the maximum number of messages a vertex may send per round to each input neighbor, and the global capacity is the maximum number of global messages it may send, and also receive, per round. The standard capacity is local capacity $O(1)$ and global capacity $O(\log n)$. A well-formed tree (WFT) is a virtual tree of maximum degree $O(1)$ and diameter $O(\log n)$. Known algorithms construct a spanning tree (ST) and a WFT either in $O(\log n)$ rounds with global capacity $O(\log^2 n)$ or with standard capacity in $O(\log^2 n)$ rounds. We give a randomized algorithm that constructs an ST and a WFT in every connected component of any graph in $O(\log n)$ rounds with high probability under standard capacity. Our approach is based on a $Δ$-pseudo-spanning representation ($Δ$-PSR): a virtual network of maximum degree $Δ$ with restoration information, such that any spanning tree of this network can be restored to a spanning tree of the input graph in $O(\log n)$ rounds. The algorithm of Götte et al. can be viewed as constructing an $O(\log n)$-PSR, which accounts for its global capacity $O(\log^2 n)$. Our main contribution is to construct an $O(1)$-PSR in $O(\log n)$ rounds with standard capacity. As applications, for $k$ distinct edge weights and any integer $1\le p\le k$, we construct an exact minimum spanning tree in $O((k/p)\log n)$ rounds with local capacity $O(p)$ and global capacity $O(p\log n)$, and the same tradeoff applies to $(1+ε)$-approximate minimum spanning trees. We also compute biconnected components, articulation points, and bridges in $O(\log n)$ rounds with standard capacity, down from the previous global capacity $O(\log^5 n)$.

title: CarrierKV: An Edge LLM Accelerator with Positional Carrier Decomposition for Low-Bit KV Cache
summary: Long-context decoding on edge devices is limited by DRAM, because every generated token reads the whole, growing KV cache. 4-bit block-scaled formats such as NVFP4 reduce this traffic but degrade accuracy: on Qwen3-4B, NVFP4 lowers 32K RULER (seven tasks) from 92.6 to 79.4, and a Hadamard rotation lowers it further to 57.7. We observe that most of the key energy is a positional carrier, one per-head vector that rotary position embedding (RoPE) rotates with position. In NVFP4, it sets the shared scale of most key blocks and lowers the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio of the content by about 5 dB, nearly one bit, yet it depends only on that vector and the position. We therefore introduce positional carrier decomposition, which removes the carrier before RoPE and stores only the content residual. We design a KV path that rotates and quantizes keys only after this removal and computes each attention score directly on the 4-bit code. We also design a positional phase engine that regenerates the carrier's score term for one key per cycle. At the same cache size as NVFP4, CarrierKV raises 32K RULER on Qwen3-4B from 79.4 to 91.1 and lowers the 32K PG19 perplexity increase of NVFP4 by 1.8 to 5.9 times on four models, outperforming SageAttention and P3-LLM on all four. Its loss also stays nearly flat as the cache grows, while that of NVFP4 rises. In a 22 nm FDSOI process at 600 MHz, CarrierKV's hardware increases the area of the NVFP4 accelerator by 2.9% and the energy of a 20K-token reasoning request on Qwen3-4B by 0.12% at the same decode latency. On Qwen3-4B at 32K, CarrierKV has a better RULER score than FP8 keys (91.1 against 89.3) and uses 13.7% less energy per token. The decomposition also lowers the 32K perplexity increase of 3-bit TurboQuant keys on Qwen3-4B from 69.7 to 0.76.

title: AceVLN: Asynchronous Cloud Edge Deployment of VLNs via Latent Scheduling and Compensation
summary: Cloud--edge deployment enables asynchronous dual-system VLN on resource-constrained robots, but inference and communication delays cause latent mismatch and navigation errors. Existing adaptation methods reuse historical guidance but cannot provide updated navigation information when it becomes inadequate. We propose AceVLN, a training-free framework for active latent refresh and edge-side compensation. Our analysis reveals that action-relevant mismatch is concentrated in a compact Critical Subspace and can be tracked through fast-system feature drift. Critical Feature Drift Entropy reflects navigation sensitivity and guides adaptive refresh, while Critical Drift Continuity indicates when recent latent updates can support compensation during latency spikes. AceVLN integrates subspace-decoupled mismatch modeling, entropy-guided refresh scheduling, and continuity-guided compensation. Experiments show that \textit{AceVLN} improves success rates by 1.7--2.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines, while reducing amortized computation time by 2.7--10.0\% and FLOPs by 18.4--22.3\%.

title: IsoMoE: Placement-Invariant Hybrid CPU-GPU MoE Inference with Lossless 12-bit Experts
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity at low computational cost. Hybrid CPU-GPU inference offloads some experts to the CPU, enabling a single GPU to run MoE models larger than its memory. Expert placement changes with free GPU memory and should only affect speed. However, the greedy decoding outputs of existing hybrid engines change with placement. This is because the two devices use different arithmetic to compute experts. In addition, decoding is limited by CPU memory bandwidth. Lossless compression reduces memory traffic, but the CPU decompresses entropy-coded formats too slowly to keep up with memory reads. To address these challenges, we propose IsoMoE, an efficient hybrid MoE inference system that guarantees that its outputs do not change with expert placement. IsoMoE introduces (i) a GPU expert kernel that bitwise replays the arithmetic of the CPU expert kernel, (ii) a memory layout that allows the CPU to efficiently compute lossless 12-bit experts using AVX-512 dot-product instructions, and (iii) a dual micro-batch pipeline that overlaps CPU and GPU computation without changing the outputs. Experimental results on three MoE models show that IsoMoE produces bitwise identical outputs across different expert placements. It is also faster than the fastest baseline in every setting, achieving an average decoding speedup of 1.26$\times$ and a maximum speedup of 1.54$\times$. Our source code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/isomoe-artifact-9C21/.

title: Stratum: A Hardware-Software Co-Design Framework for SNN Inference on RISC-V
summary: Efficient spiking neural network (SNN) inference on RISC-V processors requires tracing implementation costs back to the compiler and hardware decisions that produce them. Training environments, compilers, and cycle-level simulators, however, typically operate as distinct tools, making this attribution difficult. This paper presents Stratum, a framework that integrates an snnTorch-trained SNN, an MLIR-based compiler stack, and a cycle-level gem5-based RISC-V model into a unified workflow. Stratum exposes two optimization levers, software decisions in the generated code and hardware configuration choices in the simulated core, and uses stage-level cycle measurements to identify performance bottlenecks. We demonstrate Stratum on a two-layer N-MNIST network with three controlled comparisons: (i)~dense vs.\ spike-gated lowering of \texttt{snn.linear}, (ii)~output-outer vs.\ spike-major weight layout with spike-gating enabled in both binaries, and (iii)~L2 cache capacity with both layouts. Our spike-gated lowering reduces simulated inference time by $64\times$ (453.2\,ms to 7.04\,ms), and our spike-major layout cuts it by a further 37.2\% (to 4.42\,ms) at 4\,MiB L2, with the predicted class unchanged. The layout speedup grows from $1.59\times$ to $1.88\times$ when L2 shrinks to 1\,MiB. These results show that Stratum enables rapid early evaluation of design choices at both the software level (compiler stack) and the hardware level (cycle-level gem5 simulation).

title: Asynchronous Byzantine Lattice Agreement with Logarithmic Response Time and Optimal Resilience
summary:
Lattice agreement is a fundamental coordination primitive in which processes decide on comparable values rather than identical ones. In the asynchronous message-passing setting with Byzantine failures, existing algorithms either require authentication or do not simultaneously achieve optimal resilience and logarithmic response time.
  We present an asynchronous Byzantine lattice agreement algorithm that tolerates up to $f$ Byzantine failures among $n>3f$ processes, requires no authentication, and completes in $O(\log f)$ time. The algorithm builds on the classifier-tree framework of Attiya and Rachman, replacing shared-memory communication with quorum-based message passing.
  The main challenge is preserving the information-flow invariants underlying the classifier tree despite Byzantine behavior. To address this challenge, we introduce Supported Reliable Broadcast (SRB), a communication abstraction that combines reliable broadcast with protocol-specific admissibility checks. Messages are disseminated using reliable broadcast, but are delivered to the protocol only after verifying that they are consistent with previously propagated information about the sender's state. This prevents Byzantine processes from bypassing the information-flow guarantees required by the classifier tree.
  A central technical difficulty lies in breaking the apparent circular dependency between message delivery and admissibility: admissibility depends on local state established by previously delivered messages, while message delivery itself depends on admissibility. Our proof resolves this circularity by separating reliable dissemination from admissibility propagation, yielding a modular correctness argument.

title: Weave: Routing-Adaptive Runtime Warp Scheduling for MoE Megakernels
summary: The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture is widely used in mainstream large language models. Under expert parallelism (EP), state-of-the-art systems fuse each MoE layer into a persistent megakernel for high performance. By the nature of EP, each GPU's communication and computation volumes vary with the routing result. However, prior work either fixes how GPU resources are divided between communication and computation at compile time (e.g., MegaMoE), or adapts to runtime dynamism only at coarse-grained SM granularity (e.g., mKernel), dedicating whole SMs to communication and leaving their Tensor Cores idle. At the finer warp granularity within each SM, static warp schedules can neither match routing-dependent loads nor prevent warps from idling while waiting for inputs or after finishing their assigned work. Therefore, we propose Weave, an MoE megakernel with three key designs. First, a spatial schedule allocates resources between communication and computation at both SM and warp granularities to match each GPU's load. Second, a temporal schedule switches warp roles as execution progresses, enlisting all warps at the start and end of a layer and selectively handing output scatter to idle communication warps. Third, a fused cost model jointly selects both schedules per GPU at launch from runtime routing statistics. Across all evaluated platforms, Weave outperforms the strongest baselines: under EP8 over DeepGEMM-MegaMoE, it speeds up the MoE layer by 1.30x geomean and up to 1.97x on SM103, and by 1.24x geomean and up to 1.72x on SM90; under EP16 on CDNA3, it beats the fastest official RCCL+AITER baseline by 1.44x geomean (up to 2.87x; 1.67x over vLLM).

title: Cruella: A Unified Microscaling and Floating-Point Dot-Product Unit for LLM Inference on FPGAs
summary: The number formats that accelerators execute natively are fixed at fabrication, yet large language model (LLM) checkpoints are released with MXFP4 weights in the Microscaling (MX) formats standardized in 2023. FPGAs adopt new formats through bitstreams. However, to the best of our knowledge, no deployed FPGA LLM accelerator executes MXFP4 weights alongside BF16 products. We characterize the decoding of MXFP4 checkpoints, whose layers alternate between MXFP4$\times$BF16 products and BF16$\times$BF16 products of attention and BF16 layers. With a BF16 KV cache, BF16$\times$BF16 products take 56%-77% of the datapath time, during which a separate MXFP4 unit idles. We present Cruella, whose unified dot-product unit (UDPU) executes both product types on one DSP array and reduction pipeline. First, per-group pre-alignment keeps this pipeline at the BF16 width and changes perplexity by at most 0.7%. Second, pre-adder packing places two signed MXFP4$\times$BF16 products in one DSP48E2 multiplier with an exact correction. On an Alveo U55C, the UDPU needs 23% fewer DSP slices and 36% fewer LUTs than separate MXFP4 and BF16 units of equal throughput. On this board, MXFP4 weights speed up decoding by 1.15$\times$-1.87$\times$ over BF16 weights, and an NVIDIA A40 GPU decodes faster but spends 0.92$\times$-2.01$\times$ the board's energy per token.

title: FOREST: Coordinating Tree-based HBF, RRAM, and HBM for Efficient Speculative LLM Inference
summary:
Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by combining lightweight drafting with parallel target-model verification. However, its stages impose distinct resource demands: target verification requires high-throughput access to large weight sets, sequential drafting executes a compact model under tight latency constraints, and long-context attention processes growing key-value (KV) caches. Conventional GPU-centric SD systems serve these workloads through shared HBM-centric memory and general-purpose compute, creating mismatches in capacity, bandwidth, and computation. These mismatches constrain deployable model-context configurations and limit the efficiency of bandwidth-bound and latency-sensitive operations.
  We propose FOREST, a heterogeneous memory-centric architecture coordinating HBF, 3D-stacked RRAM, and HBM memory-compute trees for efficient SD. It features: (1) compute-aligned 3D RRAM, combining ultra-wide, low-frequency reads with clock-decoupled interfaces and overlapped SRAM-DCIM weight refills for latency-sensitive drafting; (2) cross-tree numerical co-design, moving block-scaled Q/K/V preprocessing to HBF and RRAM root plates and enabling block-floating-point (BFP) attention with pipelined softmax reduction in the HBM tree; and (3) HBF-aware SD design-space exploration, revealing how bandwidth-compute provisioning and model scale determine performance, energy, and cost trade-offs. Evaluated across six SD configurations spanning 32B-405B target models, FOREST achieves up to 5.5x end-to-end speedup, 11.46x higher decode throughput, and 16.5x higher decode energy efficiency over NVIDIA A800 GPU-based SD baselines. Under a modeled total cost of ownership, FOREST delivers up to 6.73x higher token-generation cost efficiency.
